title: Sumer: Writing, Cities and the First Laws

cards.h: Writing was invented to count beer and barley
cards.b:
The most important invention in history started as boring accounting. Around 3300 BCE, in a city called Uruk, someone pressed a reed into wet clay to record who owed what.

Welcome to Sumer, in southern Mesopotamia, the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

Sumer had city-states such as Uruk, Ur, Lagash and Kish. By about 3000 BCE, Uruk may have held tens of thousands of people. Each city had its own god, its own king and a temple tower called a ziggurat.

Farmers used canals to irrigate barley fields in a hot, dry land. Controlling water meant organising people. That helped create governments.
The word cuneiform means 'wedge-shaped'. At first it recorded rations and goods. Later it carried letters, poems, spells and laws. Scribes trained for years in schools called edubba.

cards.h: The first named author was a woman
cards.b:
Enheduanna (about 2300 BCE) was a priestess and daughter of King Sargon of Akkad. She wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna and signed them. She is the first author we know by name.

Sargon himself created the first big empire, the Akkadian empire, joining many city-states under one ruler. He is a legend in his own right: the story says he was found as a baby floating in a basket on a river.

The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest stories we still have. Gilgamesh was a king of Uruk, probably a real ruler. In the poem he seeks eternal life after his friend Enkidu dies.

The epic includes a great flood, long before the Bible's Noah story was written down. The version we know best was written about 1200-1000 BCE, based on older Sumerian stories.

The oldest surviving law code is that of Ur-Nammu of Ur (about 2100 BCE). The most famous is Hammurabi's of Babylon (about 1754 BCE), carved on a black stone pillar now in the Louvre in Paris.

Hammurabi's laws often punished by 'eye for an eye'. But punishment depended on rank: harming a noble cost more than harming a commoner.

cards.h: Was Hammurabi's code the first law?
cards.b: Myth: Hammurabi wrote the world's first laws.Fact: Ur-Nammu's and others came centuries earlier. Hammurabi's is simply the best preserved. Historians also argue about whether it was a law book used in courts or a royal showpiece that praised the king as a just ruler. Both could be true.

Five things to remember

  1. Writing began in Uruk around 3300 BCE as accounting.
  2. Cuneiform was used for about 3,000 years.
  3. Enheduanna is the first named author.
  4. Gilgamesh is among the oldest epics.
  5. Ur-Nammu's laws predate Hammurabi's by centuries.

Think about it

  • Why might rulers want laws written in stone?
  • What does it say about power that writing started with accounts?
